items.parameter: Distribution functions: general rule
items.value: These are built-in functions that return random values from a distribution. Any numeric expression accepts them, including process times, arrival frequency, Qty each and variable assignment.
items.quote: Distribution functions are built-in functions which, in conjunction with streams, return random values according to a statistical distribution. They are valid in any numeric expression.
items.source: MedModel 8.6 Online Help (same language engine as ProModel 8.6), Logic Elements > Distribution Functions. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Exponential E()
items.value: E(a{,<s>,<ax>}): a = mean (not rate). Takes an optional stream <s> and an optional axis shift <ax>.
items.quote: To use an Exponential distribution interval, use the syntax E(mean), where mean is the average amount for your interval.
items.source: ProModel docs, Distribution Intervals (docs.promodel.com/pmacad). Seen only in a WebSearch extract. The full syntax 'E(a{,<s>,<ax>})' also appeared in the MedModel 8.6 Distribution Functions extract.

items.parameter: Normal N()
items.value: N(a,b{,<s>}): a = mean, b = standard deviation. There is no axis shift. Negative draws used as times are set to zero (see the time-expression item).
items.quote: Normal ... N(a,b{,<s>}) ... a=mean, b=standard deviation (table row as reproduced in the search extract); help example: 'defined by a normal distribution with a mean value of ... minutes and a standard deviation of ... minutes, N(...)'
items.source: MedModel 8.6 / ProModel 8.0 Online Help, Distribution Functions table; downtime example in ProModel 8.0 help. Seen only in WebSearch extracts. Example numbers omitted because the page was not opened.

items.parameter: Triangular T()
items.value: T(a,b,c{,<s>}): a = minimum, b = mode, c = maximum. The mode is the middle argument.
items.quote: The syntax is T(minimum, mode, maximum), and the mode is the amount that occurs most often (note that this is not the same as the mean).
items.source: ProModel docs, Distribution Intervals. Seen only in a WebSearch extract, and the extract may be lightly paraphrased.

items.parameter: Uniform U()
items.value: U(a,b{,<s>}): a = MEAN, b = HALF-RANGE. This is not (min, max). Uniform[min, max] is written U((min+max)/2, (max-min)/2).
items.quote: To use a Uniform distribution interval, use the syntax U(mean, half range) ... The half range is the amount above or below the mean that can occur.
items.source: ProModel docs, Distribution Intervals. Seen only in a WebSearch extract. The MedModel 8.6 Distribution Functions extract also gave 'U(a,b{,<s>}) ... a=mean, b=half range'.

items.parameter: Lognormal L(): parameter meaning
items.value: L(a,b{,<s>,<ax>}): the documentation labels a 'mean' and b 'standard deviation'. None of the extracts says whether these describe the lognormal variable itself or the underlying normal of ln(x). Two things point to the lognormal's own arithmetic moments, but this is NOT confirmed: the help's worked example states the mean and standard deviation in minutes, and the sibling product ProcessModel documents Stat::Fit converting mu/sigma into the data's mean and SD. Run a test in ProModel to settle it (see proposed_distributions).
items.quote: Lognormal | L(a,b{,<s>,<ax>}) | a=mean, b=standard deviation; help example: 'the setup time for the machine will be based on a Lognormal distribution with a mean of ... minutes and a standard deviation of ... min'
items.source: ProModel 8.0 Online Help, Distribution Functions and Setup Downtime Editor; ProModel docs, Distribution Intervals ('Lognormal | L(a,b) | a=mean, b=standard deviation'). Seen only in WebSearch extracts. Example numbers omitted.

items.parameter: Weibull W()
items.value: W(a,b{,<s>,<ax>}): a = SHAPE, b = SCALE. This matches scipy weibull_min(c=shape, scale=scale). The location goes into the axis shift <ax>, which needs a stream.
items.quote: Weibull | W(a,b) | a=shape value, b=scale value
items.source: ProModel docs, Distribution Intervals; MedModel 8.6 Distribution Functions ('W(a,b{,<s>,<ax>})'). Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: Gamma G()
items.value: G(a,b{,<s>,<ax>}): a = SHAPE, b = SCALE. This matches scipy gamma(a, scale). The documentation says 'scale value', so the mean is a*b. That is my inference; the docs do not state the mean.
items.quote: Gamma | G(a,b) | a=shape value, b=scale value
items.source: ProModel docs, Distribution Intervals; MedModel 8.6 Distribution Functions ('G(a,b{,<s>,<ax>})'). Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: Erlang ER()
items.value: ER(a,b{,<s>}): a = mean, b = integer shape parameter (k). The docs do not say whether 'mean' is the whole Erlang or one phase. Assume the whole Erlang (total mean = a) and verify. No axis shift.
items.quote: Erlang | ER(a,b) | a=mean, b=integer shape parameter
items.source: ProModel docs, Distribution Intervals. The MedModel 8.6 extract gives 'a=mean value, b=parameter'. Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: Beta B()
items.value: B(a,b,c,d{,<s>}): a = shape 1, b = shape 2, c = lower bound, d = upper bound. This is a generalized beta on [c, d].
items.quote: Beta | B(a,b,c,d) | a=shape value 1, b=shape value 2, c=lower boundary, d=upper boundary
items.source: ProModel docs, Distribution Intervals. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Poisson P()
items.value: P(a{,<s>}): a single parameter that the docs label 'quantity'. It is the Poisson mean (lambda). Draws are integers, so P() suits a daily-count Qty each.
items.quote: Poisson | P(a{,<s>}) | a=quantity
items.source: MedModel 8.6 Online Help, Distribution Functions. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Binomial BI()
items.value: BI(a,b{,<s>}): a = batch size (number of trials n), b = probability of success p.
items.quote: BI(a,b{,<s>}): Binomial, where a is the batch size and b is the probability of success (the extract paraphrased the table row 'a=batch size, b=probability of success')
items.source: MedModel 8.6 Online Help, Distribution Functions. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Geometric GEO()
items.value: GEO(a{,<s>}): a = probability of success.
items.quote: GEO(a{,<s>}): Geometric, where a is the probability of success (paraphrase of the table row)
items.source: MedModel 8.6 Online Help, Distribution Functions. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Inverse Gaussian IG(), Pearson5 P5(), Pearson6 P6()
items.value: IG(a,b{,<s>,<ax>}): a = shape, b = scale. P5(a,b{,<s>,<ax>}): a = shape, b = scale. P6(a,b,c{,<s>,<ax>}): a = shape 1, b = shape 2, c = scale.
items.quote: Inverse Gaussian · IG(a,b) · a=shape value b=scale value ... Weibull · W(a,b) · a=shape value b=scale value; P6(a,b,c{,<s>,<ax>}) two shape values then a scale value
items.source: ProModel Process Simulator Help, Distributions; MedModel 8.6 Distribution Functions. Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: Stream argument <s>
items.value: The optional stream index is the next argument after the distribution parameters. If it is omitted, the software uses stream 1. If no seed is set, a stream's seed equals its stream number. Give independent inputs (arrivals, kWh, dwell) separate streams for common-random-numbers comparisons.
items.quote: If no stream is given, MedModel will use stream one. / If you do not specify an initial seed value, ProModel will use the stream number as the seed value (i.e., stream 3 uses seed 3).
items.source: MedModel 8.6 Distribution Functions; ProModel 8.6 Help, Using Random Number Streams. Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: Axis shift <ax> (location parameter)
items.value: E, G, W, L, IG, P5 and P6 start at 0 by default. A location or shift goes in <ax>, and the stream must also be given, e.g. W(shape, scale, 3, loc).
items.quote: The distributions, E, G, W, L, IG, P5, and P6 all normally have a minimum value of zero ... Any time an axis shift is specified, a stream must be specified also.
items.source: MedModel 8.6 Online Help, Distribution Functions. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Negative draws in time expressions
items.value: When N(), T() and similar return a negative value used as a time, ProModel silently sets it to 0. This is a truncation, so the realized mean shifts upward. Use L, W or G for strictly positive durations.
items.quote: any negative value returned by a distribution that is used for a time expression will be automatically converted to zero
items.source: ProModel 8.0 Online Help, Distribution Functions > General Components; also Time Expressions (8.6). Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: User-defined distributions (empirical tables)
items.value: Defined in Build > More Elements > User Distributions. Fields: ID (name), Type = Discrete or Continuous, Cumulative = Yes or No, and a Table of value/percent rows. Call it like a function with empty parentheses, e.g. kWh_Req().
items.quote: The name of the distribution. Discrete or Continuous depending on the number of possible outcomes. Yes or No depending on whether the distribution is to be specified in cumulative or non-cumulative format. ... the open and closed parentheses after the distribution name must be used, such as Dist1(), OpTime().
items.source: ProModel 8.0 Online Help, User Distribution Edit Table and User Defined Distributions. Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: Continuous user distribution: table semantics
items.value: In cumulative form, each row is (x, P(X <= x)) and the first row is the minimum with 0%. In non-cumulative form, each row gives the probability mass of the range ending at that x. Values between break points are drawn within the range, i.e. a piecewise-linear CDF. That interpolation is my inference; the extract does not state it.
items.quote: a cumulative distribution specifies the probability that an observed value will be less than or equal to a specified value ... P(2.0 <= X < 3.5) = 0.20 (help example of the density form)
items.source: ProModel 8.0 Online Help, User Defined Distributions > Continuous Distributions. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Arrival Cycles: definition table
items.value: Defined in Build > More Elements > Arrival Cycles. Fields: ID; Qty/% (Percent or Quantity basis); Cumulative (Yes/No); Table (time-of-cycle break points with a percent or quantity per interval). Time values in the table are always cumulative, measured from the start of the cycle.
items.quote: Select either Percent or Quantity as the basis for the total number of arrivals per cycle occurrence. ... Select Yes to specify the % or Qty values in a cumulative format. ... Time values remain cumulative regardless of the form of the percentages.
items.source: ProModel 8.0 Online Help, Arrival Cycles Edit Table and Cumulative Cycle Tables. Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: Arrival Cycles: within-interval timing
items.value: Within each cycle interval, arrival times are drawn UNIFORMLY over that interval. They are not exponential or Poisson. The time-varying rate is therefore piecewise-constant, with uniform placement inside each block.
items.quote: The arrivals are randomly distributed according to a Uniform distribution during the time interval in which they arrive.
items.source: ProModel 8.6 Online Help, Arrival Cycles Example. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Arrival Cycles: hooking a cycle into an Arrivals record
items.value: In the Arrivals table, put the cycle name (optionally followed by a quantity) in Qty Each. Occurrences = number of cycle repetitions (e.g. number of simulated days). Frequency = time between cycle starts (e.g. 24 hr), in the same time unit as the cycle.
items.quote: If you have previously created an arrival cycle and want to use it for this arrival, enter the name of the arrival cycle followed optionally by a quantity. ... If an arrival cycle is used, this is the number of times to repeat the cycle. ... If an arrival cycle was entered for the arrival quantity, this is the time between the start of each cycle.
items.source: ProModel 8.6 / 8.0 Online Help, Arrivals Edit Table. Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: Arrival Cycles: Percent vs Quantity basis and the Qty Each meaning
items.value: With a Percent basis, Qty Each is the total arrivals per cycle, which the percent table splits across intervals. With a Quantity basis, Qty Each is a multiplier applied to every table entry. Qty Each may be any expression that evaluates to a number; the docs do not confirm whether a distribution there is re-sampled each cycle.
items.quote: An arrival cycle will divide the quantity specified in the Qty each... field into various sized groups arriving throughout the day. / the Qty each field in the Arrivals table represents a factor by which all entries in the cycle table will be multiplied. ... This field may be any valid expression which evaluates to a number.
items.source: ProModel 8.6 Arrival Cycles Example; ProModel 8.0 Arrival Cycles by Quantity. Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: External Arrivals file (trace-driven arrivals)
items.value: Declared in Build > More Elements > External Files with type Arrival. Columns A-F: entity name, location name, quantity per arrival, time of first arrival, number of occurrences, frequency. Columns G onward set attributes when the header matches an attribute name (e.g. kWh_req, dwell). The 8.0 help allows .wk1/.xls only; the 9.3 help says Excel. Cells must hold values, not spreadsheet formulas, because a formula cell is read as 0. Rows are read in after the Arrivals-editor data. This lets each ACN session be replayed as one row.
items.quote: The values in the spreadsheet cells must be a numeric expression as opposed to a formula commonly used in spreadsheets. For example, if cell E4 in the spreadsheet above was actually a formula generating the value 100, the value ProModel generates is zero.
items.source: ProModel 8.0 Online Help, External Files > File Types > Arrivals File; ProModel 9.3 Help, File Types. Seen only in WebSearch extracts.

items.parameter: External Arrivals in Process Simulator (sibling product)
items.value: Process Simulator accepts .xls or .xlsx. The first row must be a header row, and only the first sheet is read. ProModel's own arrivals file probably behaves the same way, but that is unconfirmed.
items.quote: An External Arrivals file is a spreadsheet (.xsl or .xlsx format only) ... The first row in the spreadsheet must be used as a header row. ... only the first sheet will be read in.
items.source: ProModel Process Simulator 9.2 Help, External Arrivals. Seen only in a WebSearch extract.

items.parameter: Stat::Fit lognormal export convention (sibling product evidence)
items.value: Stat::Fit fits a lognormal as [min, mu, sigma], where mu and sigma belong to the underlying normal. ProcessModel takes the mean and SD of the data after the offset, and Stat::Fit's Distribution Viewer converts between the two. The extract's 'sd' formula is actually the variance (take its square root). This supports, but does not prove, that ProModel's L(a,b) also expects arithmetic moments.
items.quote: For the Lognormal distribution, Stat::Fit uses the parameters [min, mu, sigma] where min is the offset from 0, and mu, sigma are the mean and standard deviation of the included normal distribution.
items.source: ProcessModel Knowledge Base, 'How does ProcessModel Convert Lognormal Conversion From Stat::Fit?' Seen only in a WebSearch extract. Another ProcessModel help page was summarized as using Lognormal(logMean, logSd), which conflicts.

proposed_distributions.model_input: ProModel lognormal convention check (do this before entering any L())
proposed_distributions.distribution: Test model: one entity type, arrivals E(1) min, process 'WAIT L(10,5)' with a stream, 10,000 entities; log each sampled time to a variable or an output file
proposed_distributions.parameters: If the sample mean is about 10 and the SD about 5, L(a,b) takes arithmetic moments. If the sample mean is about exp(10+12.5), it takes log-scale parameters.
proposed_distributions.basis: The documentation labels 'a=mean, b=standard deviation' without saying which scale (unverified extract). The test is our assumption and costs about 5 minutes.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Move-after-charge response delay (repo synthesis.py: lognormal, median d, sigma 0.8)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Lognormal via ProModel L()
proposed_distributions.parameters: If L takes arithmetic moments: L(1.377*d, 1.304*d), from mean = d*exp(0.8^2/2) and SD = mean*sqrt(exp(0.8^2)-1). If it takes log-scale: L(ln d, 0.8). d = 0 means skip the WAIT (valet case).
proposed_distributions.basis: The sigma 0.8 and median d are the repo's own assumptions (codespace/unobserved_behavior/synthesis.py). The conversion is standard lognormal algebra. The ProModel L() semantics come from an unverified documentation extract.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Waitlist move-in time after a port frees (repo: Uniform(0, hold))
proposed_distributions.distribution: Uniform via ProModel U(mean, half-range)
proposed_distributions.parameters: U(hold/2, hold/2) min. With the ChargePoint 15-min hold: U(7.5, 7.5) min. With the Cal Poly 30-min hold: U(15, 15) min.
proposed_distributions.basis: Hold times are the already-verified facts (ChargePoint 15 min, Cal Poly 30 min). Using Uniform(0, hold) is the repo's assumption. That ProModel's U is (mean, half-range) comes from an unverified documentation extract.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Waitlist patience / retry delay (repo: exponential, mean theta)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Exponential via ProModel E(mean)
proposed_distributions.parameters: E(theta) min. Shifted form: E(theta, s, shift).
proposed_distributions.basis: Theta is a repo assumption. That E takes the mean, not the rate, comes from an unverified documentation extract.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Any Weibull or Gamma fit from scipy (e.g. dwell or kWh fitted on ACN)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Weibull or Gamma
proposed_distributions.parameters: scipy weibull_min(c, loc, scale) maps to W(c, scale, s, loc). scipy gamma(a, loc, scale) maps to G(a, scale, s, loc). Give each input its own stream s.
proposed_distributions.basis: ProModel argument order is shape then scale, with location in <ax> requiring a stream (unverified extract). The scipy parameter names are standard.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Time-of-day arrival profile (ACN hourly connection counts)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Non-homogeneous arrivals via an Arrival Cycle
proposed_distributions.parameters: Arrival Cycle with Percent basis, Cumulative = No, 24 one-hour rows holding each hour's ACN share of daily arrivals. Arrivals record: Qty Each = '<cycle> <daily count>'; Frequency = 24 hr; Occurrences = number of simulated days (or weekdays only, using separate weekday/weekend cycles). Arrivals are uniform within each hour.
proposed_distributions.basis: The cycle mechanics are an unverified documentation extract. The hourly shares should be computed from ACN data. Whether Qty Each = P(lambda) is re-sampled each day is undocumented; if it is not, generate daily counts through an external arrivals file instead.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Trace-driven validation run (replay real ACN sessions)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Empirical trace via an External Arrivals file
proposed_distributions.parameters: One row per ACN session. A = EV entity, B = arrival location, C = 1, D = connection time (in model time units from the run start), E = 1, F = 0. G onward = attribute columns such as kWh_req and planned_dwell, with headers equal to the attribute names. Write values only, no formulas.
proposed_distributions.basis: The file layout is from an unverified documentation extract (ProModel 8.0/9.3 help). The ACN fields come from the team's own data.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Empirical kWh requested or dwell time, where no parametric fit is adequate
proposed_distributions.distribution: Continuous user-defined distribution
proposed_distributions.parameters: Type = Continuous, Cumulative = Yes. Rows are (x_i, F(x_i)) at about 10-20 ACN quantiles with the first row at 0%. Call it as kWh_Req().
proposed_distributions.basis: Mechanics are from an unverified documentation extract. The quantiles should come from ACN data.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Per-port time to failure (TTF) for each Level-2 EVSE (ProModel clock-based downtime frequency on the EVSE location/resource)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Exponential (constant hazard)
proposed_distributions.parameters: Mean MTBF = MTTR * A / (1 - A). Baseline A = 0.97 and MTTR = 7 d give MTBF = 226.3 d = 5,432 h, so use E(5432) hr. If your ProModel version measures downtime frequency start-to-start rather than end-to-start, use E(5600) hr (MTBF + MTTR). Implications for 54 ports: on average 1.62 ports down at any time, about 84.5 port failures per year garage-wide, and P(a port fails during a 10 h connection) = 1 - exp(-10/5432) = 0.18%.
proposed_distributions.basis: A = 0.97 is the NEVI floor in 23 CFR 680.116 (more than 97% port uptime for publicly funded chargers; verified earlier in this workflow). It is a regulatory floor, not a measurement, and it does not bind a private workplace garage. MTTR = 7 d is an ASSUMPTION, because no Level-2 repair-time measurement could be opened (see 'unopened'). The exponential shape is also an ASSUMPTION: no opened source gives a hazard shape for Level-2 EVSE. Long-run availability depends only on the two means, so the exponential choice does not bias A. MTBF is computed from these inputs, not sourced.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Repair / outage duration per failure (ProModel downtime logic: WAIT <repair time>)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Lognormal (right-skewed); exponential as a simpler fallback
proposed_distributions.parameters: Mean 168 h (7 d) and SD 168 h (CV = 1). In ProModel this is L(168,168) hr, where ProModel's L(a,b) takes the lognormal's own mean and SD (check this in your version's help). Underlying normal parameters (ln-hours): mu = 4.777, sigma = 0.833, which gives median about 119 h (5 d) and 90th percentile about 345 h (14 d). Sensitivity range for the mean: 24 h to 720 h (1-30 d). Fallback: E(168) hr.
proposed_distributions.basis: ENTIRELY ASSUMED. The right skew reflects qualitative operator reports that a minority of outages need several technician visits and account for a disproportionate share of downtime (ChargerHelp 2024 and 2026 reports). Those reports could not be opened, so none of their numbers are used. Replace the mean and SD once they or the Stanford 'Beyond Uptime' Level-2 case study are opened. proposed_distributions.model_input: p_balk: a driver who finds all 54 ports occupied does not wait (parks elsewhere, no charge)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Bernoulli(p_balk)
proposed_distributions.parameters: baseline p_balk = 1.0 (Erlang loss); sweep 0.5-1.0
proposed_distributions.basis: ASSUMPTION. No published workplace balking rate was found that we could open. Qualitative support: drivers avoid arriving to a full garage (Garg et al. 2026 WP), and unmanaged workplace sites simply turn late arrivals away (Sutton et al. 2022, verified earlier). ACN never came within 2 ports of full (team diagnostics), so it cannot be estimated from ACN.

proposed_distributions.model_input: On-site queue patience (impatient variant: a driver who waits in or near the car for a port)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Gamma(shape k, scale theta) truncated at 120 min; alternative Exponential(mean 44 min)
proposed_distributions.parameters: k = 1.70, theta = 25.8 min (mean 43.8, SD 33.6); lognormal alternative mu = 3.55, sigma = 0.68 (median 35 min); sweep mean 15-60 min
proposed_distributions.basis: Mean and SD SOURCED from Wang et al. 2024 (arXiv:2412.16240, stated Comfort Time, n = 230), corroborated by the 45-min saturation in the same study. The gamma shape and the truncation are our fit. Strong transferability caveat: Chinese highway, DC-fast, stated preference. Patience as 0.6 x charge time (Chattopadhyay & Kar 2024) is only an assumed alternative.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Virtual waitlist: patience and claim delay for drivers parked elsewhere
proposed_distributions.distribution: Patience = the driver's remaining planned dwell (structural). Claim delay after a 'port free' notice ~ Lognormal(median m, sigma 0.8); a driver who misses the hold window H loses the slot
proposed_distributions.parameters: H = 15 min (ChargePoint Waitlist) or 30 min (Cal Poly); m = 10 min (sweep 5-20)
proposed_distributions.basis: H SOURCED (verified earlier: ChargePoint Waitlist 15 min; Cal Poly 30 min). The claim-delay median and shape are ASSUMPTIONS (no measured waitlist response times found).

proposed_distributions.model_input: Post-charge idle with a notification only (no rule, no fee) = baseline
proposed_distributions.distribution: Empirical idle distribution resampled from ACN Caltech completed sessions, plus a small completion-triggered share rho that unplugs within Exp(10 min)
proposed_distributions.parameters: Caltech idle median 187 min; 9.3% unplug within 15 min; 74% stay > 60 min (JPL median 232 min); rho = 3.1%
proposed_distributions.basis: ACN numbers computed by the team (repo diagnostics and our site split, partial download). That a notification already exists is SOURCED (Lee et al. 2021: most vehicles notify owners when charging stops). So a 'notification-only' policy should NOT be modeled as a large behavior change unless new evidence appears.

proposed_distributions.model_input: gamma: compliance with a move-after-charge rule / time limit with fee
proposed_distributions.distribution: Bernoulli(gamma); a compliant driver unplugs by min(natural departure, deadline); a non-compliant driver overstays (next row)
proposed_distributions.parameters: '4-h limit + ~$1/h fee + etiquette' scenario: gamma = 0.85 (sweep 0.75-0.95). 'Rule, no fee': gamma = 0.6 (assumption, sweep 0.2-0.9).
proposed_distributions.basis: Fee scenario anchored on our DERIVED proxy: 88.7% of sessions ended <= 4 h at the Asensio et al. (2022) firm, with a sharp drop in sessions just after 4 h, vs 23-42% <= 4 h at ACN sites with no limit. This is not causal: some of those sessions would have ended early anyway, so 0.85 is deliberately below 0.887. Fee level ~$0.98/h after 4 h with a $0.50 minimum is also derived. The 'no fee' value is an assumption. Published effect sizes (Asensio et al. 2022; Wolbertus & Gerzon 2018; Bornioli et al. 2023) could not be opened.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Overstay beyond the deadline for non-compliant drivers
proposed_distributions.distribution: Lognormal on minutes past the deadline
proposed_distributions.parameters: mu = 3.23, sigma = 1.43 (median 25 min; empirical median 31, IQR 11-72, P90 133 min); cap at the driver's natural departure
proposed_distributions.basis: DERIVED by us from the Asensio et al. (2022) replication data (n = 378 sessions over 4 h). Workplace L2, 2014-2015.

proposed_distributions.model_input: Post-completion idle under an enforced posted limit (alternative single-distribution form)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Lognormal (or Gamma) on idle minutes after charge completion
proposed_distributions.parameters: Lognormal mu = 3.99, sigma = 0.96 (mean 85, SD 104, median 54 min); Gamma alternative k = 0.67, theta = 127 min
proposed_distributions.basis: Mean and SD SOURCED from UCSD (Garg et al. 2026 WP: 4-h/12-h limits with citations), driver-level means; the distribution shape is our assumption. proposed_distributions.model_input: Response delay after a charge-complete notice for compliant drivers (move-after-charge policy)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Grace G, then delay ~ Lognormal(median d, sigma 1.0)
proposed_distributions.parameters: G = 10-15 min; d = 15 min (sweep 5-60)
proposed_distributions.basis: ASSUMPTION, bracketed by sourced anchors: operator hold windows of 15/30 min (verified earlier), overshoot median 25-31 min in the Asensio data (derived), and 'minutes to hours' when people perform interchange (Zeng et al. 2019). No field measurement of notice-to-move delay could be opened (Bornioli et al. 2023 measured stated intentions).

proposed_distributions.model_input: Valet / attendant interchange (operator moves charged cars)
proposed_distributions.distribution: Delay ~ Uniform(5, 30) min; cost per move fixed
proposed_distributions.parameters: cost $0.44 per interchange event
proposed_distributions.basis: Cost SOURCED as a case-study parameter (Zeng, Zhang & Moura 2019, arXiv:1901.07110), not a measurement. The delay range is an ASSUMPTION.

proposed_distributions.model_input: p_retry: a blocked driver comes back later the same day
proposed_distributions.distribution: Bernoulli(p_retry); return delay ~ Exponential(mean mu_r), truncated before the driver's departure; at most one retry
proposed_distributions.parameters: baseline p_retry = 0 (does not understate lost demand); sweep 0-0.5; mu_r = 150 min (sweep 60-240)
proposed_distributions.basis: ASSUMPTION. No quantitative retry rate found in any source we could open. Qualitative only: a workplace driver re-checks around lunchtime (Sutton et al. 2022, verified earlier), and drivers shift plug-in timing under scarcity (Garg et al. 2026 WP). The latter suggests modeling 'shift tomorrow's arrival' (R05) as the main alternative to same-day retry.

In this model, gamma only matters for drivers whose natural departure is later than the deadline (compliers leave at min(natural, deadline)). So gamma should be about 1 - P(>4h | rule) / P(>4h | no rule), not the share of sessions <= 4h. With the team's ACN no-rule shares over 4 h (58.1% Caltech, 77.4% JPL), that gives about 0.81 and 0.85. If the 2014-15 firm's own counterfactual share over 4 h was lower (smaller batteries), the implied gamma is lower (e.g. a 30% counterfactual gives about 0.62). Therefore 0.85 is not 'deliberately below 0.887' and is not conservative. Restate the logic and widen the sweep to about 0.6-0.95. State the fee as the authors' scheduled rule ($0.50 for 4-4.5 h, then $1/h in 5-min steps), not as a derived ~$0.98. 'Rule, no fee' = 0.6 is correctly labeled as an assumption. Note that the replication script also analyzes a 2-h 'Behavioral' threshold with no visible bunching (only 20% of sessions <= 2 h), but what that threshold means is unverified.

distribution_review.model_input: Overstay beyond the deadline for non-compliant drivers
distribution_review.note: Use the MLE values mu = 3.24, sigma = 1.45 (median 25.5); the empirical quantiles match exactly. This is defensible for a 'limit + fee' scenario. Label it as non-compliers who paid about $1/h, at a 4-h plug-in-based deadline. Transferring it to a deadline set by charge completion is an assumption.

distribution_review.model_input: Post-completion idle under an enforced posted limit (UCSD-based lognormal/gamma)
distribution_review.note: The moment arithmetic is correct (mu = 3.985, sigma = 0.957, median 53.8; Gamma k = 0.668, theta = 127). The evidence does not support the label. (1) SD 104 is the spread across drivers' weekly figures (N = 403 drivers), so a session-level fit will understate dispersion. (2) UCSD 'idle' is any plugged-in non-charging time, which at the PowerFlex EV-12 stalls includes scheduled pauses, so it is not post-completion idle. (3) EV-4 explicitly allows idling up to 4 h and EV-12 allows 12 h, so this is a loose time limit, not a move-after-charge rule, and enforcement intensity is unknown. (4) The comparison sets means (85, 75 min) against ACN medians. (5) The Cal Poly rule is unknown, so it cannot cross-check an 'under a rule' scenario. Relabel it as 'posted 4h/12h limit, mixed idle definition, driver-level moments; shape assumed', or drop it.

distribution_review.model_input: Response delay after charge-complete notice (compliant drivers)
distribution_review.note: This is labeled as an assumption. The anchors are loose. The Asensio overshoot (median 25-31 min) belongs to fee-paying non-compliers, not compliers. Zeng et al. say human interchange can take 'several minutes to several hours', so extend the sweep beyond 60 min.

distribution_review.model_input: Valet / attendant interchange
distribution_review.note: $0.44 is confirmed as an unsourced case-study input, and the basis says so correctly. The Uniform(5, 30) delay is labeled as an assumption. Zeng's footnote ('several minutes to several hours' when humans are involved) suggests 30 min is an optimistic upper bound, so sweep higher.

distribution_review.model_input: p_retry: blocked driver returns later the same day
distribution_review.note: This is labeled as an assumption, and a baseline of 0 with a sweep is defensible. Garg et al. supports making next-day re-timing (R05) the main alternative, since the paper documents anticipatory shifts under perceived scarcity, not same-day retries.

distribution_review.model_input: Price-regime multiplier on arrival rate (free <-> paid)
distribution_review.note: Making the ACN pre/post change the primary estimate is the right call. A web-search snippet of a Caltech procurement notice supports free -> $0.12/kWh from 1 Nov 2018, but I could not open the page (ENOTFOUND). Two problems remain. (1) The Palo Alto band U(0.57, 0.70) is too narrow. In the repo's own results CSV, the DiD placebo is +9.8% (CI +4 to +16), so the design has roughly ±10 pp bias, and ITS estimates vary from -28.5% to -33.7% by bandwidth. A fallback band of about U(0.55, 0.80) is more honest. The fee was also $0.23/kWh at public sites, not $0.12 at a workplace. (2) paid -> free U(1.43, 1.75) is presented as the 'reciprocal', but no source observes a fee being removed, so symmetric reversibility is an unlabeled assumption. Also, 1/U(0.57, 0.70) is not uniform. It should be labeled as an assumption, or derived as 1/m from the same draw.

distribution_review.model_input: Price-regime multipliers on per-session behavior when paid
distribution_review.note: The values are faithful to the source, and the workplace transfer is labeled as an assumption. kWh/session U(0.81, 0.86): the 2016 placebo shows a significant -7% (CI -10.6 to -3.2), so part of the drop may be secular trend; something like U(0.80, 0.95) is safer. Idle U(0.35, 0.50): the study says idle time fell because 'the fee mostly removed people who used the chargers as parking', which is a change in who charges, not a change per session. At a workplace, dwell time is set by work hours. Applying this as a per-session multiplier on top of the lower arrival rate double-counts the effect and is weakly transferable. Better to model the change in user mix, or estimate it from ACN before and after Nov 2018.

distribution_review.model_input: Demand growth factor over time
distribution_review.note: Acceptable as a scenario range. The upper bound is correct: (6.3M/1.12M)^(1/6) - 1 = 33.4%. The lower bound of 0.10 is labeled as an assumption. Caveats to state: (a) 33% is an early-adoption CAGR from a low base; total US EV sales grew only about 9% from 2023 to 2024, and the 2018-2024 sales CAGR is about 27%. (b) Compounding at fixed ports without a saturation cap explodes over long horizons (1.33^10 ≈ 17x), so cap growth by the employee pool or the port count. (c) ICCT defaults let workplace utilization rise only from 8% to 20% as EV share goes from 2% to 50%, so arrivals per port do not scale one-for-one with fleet growth.

distribution_review.model_input: Registered EV drivers per port
distribution_review.note: 1.5, 2 and 3 are labeled as assumptions; 0.81 is correct arithmetic. Two corrections to the framing. Asensio counts 'stations', not ports, and only drivers 'with repeat usage', so 0.81 is a lower bound. That program was also lightly used (about 32 sessions per station over the whole period), so 0.8 reflects under-subscription, not a design ratio. Prefer the empirical userID-per-port count from ACN Caltech as the baseline.

distribution_review.model_input: Vehicle type of an arriving EV (PHEV vs BEV)
distribution_review.note: The IEA shares are correct (39.3% in 2019, 25.4% in 2024, 42.9% in 2018). But the claim that 0.39 'matches ACN 2018-2019' has no source: ACN has no vehicle-type field. Fleet stock share is also not the share among workplace arrivals. Lee et al. 2020 report BEV owners use workplace charging more often (30-40% vs <30% for PHEV owners), and 8.9% of PHEV owners never plug in, so both push the PHEV share among arrivals below the stock share. Example: 0.393×0.30 / (0.393×0.30 + 0.607×0.35) ≈ 0.36 or lower. Present 0.39 as an upper bound, drop 'matches ACN', and do not use this Bernoulli together with the on-board-charger mixture without checking for double counting.

distribution_review.model_input: On-board charger limit class at a 6.6 kW ACN port
distribution_review.note: The assumptions are labeled; 0.515×0.646 = 0.333 is correct. Caveats: (a) q = 0.515 is larger than the PHEV stock share of 0.39, so the slow class is not purely PHEVs (early BEVs are in it too), and scaling q by the PHEV-share ratio is weakly grounded. Show it as a sensitivity case, not a forecast. (b) In an EVSE-upgrade scenario, do not apply the ICCT 0.8-0.9 delivery ratio on top of vehicle-class caps. ICCT defines that ratio as including 'vehicle charge acceptance', so it would double-count. (c) q comes from the repo's own ACN analysis and was not checked here.

distribution_review.model_input: Workplace-dependent driver segment
distribution_review.note: P(work-dependent) = 0.14-0.16 rests on a misread. The 16% in Lee et al. is the Home-work group: reading it as Work-only gives 53+13+20+16 = 102% given the paper's '86% charged from home'. The 14% is the ceiling for all non-home groups together (Work-only + Public-only + Work-public), and the text never states the Work-only share. The denominator is also all PEV owners; a workplace simulation needs the share among workplace-charger users, which the text does not give. Energy multiplier: 70/20 = 3.5 holds for BEVs only. PHEVs give 80/20 = 4.0 by energy share, but ICCT's electric-VKT shares (45% without home access vs 70% with) reduce that to 0.80×0.45 / (0.20×0.70) ≈ 2.6. ICCT shares are of annual energy, so the extra energy may show up as more sessions rather than larger ones, and each session is capped by 6.6 kW × dwell time. Re-label this as a scenario with P ≤ 0.14 (assumption) and an energy multiplier of about 2.6-3.5 (assumption).

distribution_review.model_input: Extreme 'free workplace charging' energy scenario (upper bound)
distribution_review.note: Recomputed and confirmed: 31,178 vs 6,041 kWh/day (5.16x); peak 5,055 vs 784 kW. The basis correctly says this is modeled output, not an elasticity. One extra caveat supports that: summed over the 49 home indices, home energy barely moves between the two scenarios (26,764 vs 26,525 kWh/day) while total energy rises from 42,449 to 65,900. The free-workplace scenario adds demand rather than shifting it from home, so use it only as a stress-test ceiling.
